params.question: Which of the following best explains why treating individual patients alone cannot address the disease burden of a community?

answers.text: Individual treatments are always clinically ineffective against community-level diseases

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Individual treatments are effective for the patients treated. The limitation is one of scale — individual prescriptions cannot address the environmental, socioeconomic, and behavioural determinants that produce disease patterns across a population.

answers.text: Shared health risks require collective interventions that individual clinical care cannot scale to deliver

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. When health risks like contaminated water, poor sanitation, or low vaccination uptake are shared across a community, collective interventions — not just individual prescriptions — are required to break the cycle of recurrent illness.

answers.text: Community health problems only involve communicable diseases that cannot be treated individually

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Community health encompasses both communicable and non-communicable diseases, as well as malnutrition, injuries, and maternal health. The issue is not the type of disease but the shared determinants that operate at the population level.

answers.text: Primary health centre doctors lack the training to treat patients from the community

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: PHC medical officers are trained for individual clinical care. The limitation is that even correct prescriptions cannot address root causes like contaminated water sources or low immunisation coverage that re-expose the entire community.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the case of Dr Priya: her individual prescriptions were correct, yet the same families returned month after month. The root causes — contaminated water, poor sanitation, low vaccination — operate at the community level and require collective interventions.

Exactly. Community health exists because shared determinants — environmental, social, economic — produce patterns of disease that no amount of individual treatment can interrupt without collective action.

interactions.label: What was the primary criticism levelled against the selective PHC approach (GOBI

params.question: What was the primary criticism levelled against the selective PHC approach (GOBI-FFF) proposed by Walsh and Warren in 1979?

answers.text: It included too many interventions for resource-constrained countries to implement

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Selective PHC was specifically designed to narrow the focus to a few cost-effective interventions. The criticism was the opposite — that by narrowing focus, it abandoned the integrated vision of the Alma-Ata Declaration.

answers.text: It was never endorsed by any international health organisation

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: GOBI-FFF was actively supported and implemented by UNICEF and other agencies. The criticism was conceptual — about what the approach left out — not about its institutional backing.

answers.text: It fragmented healthcare and ignored the social determinants that comprehensive PHC was designed to address

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Critics argued that cherry-picking a few vertical interventions abandoned the Alma-Ata vision of addressing health holistically — including the social, economic, and environmental determinants that produce disease.

answers.text: It focused exclusively on adult diseases and excluded maternal and child health interventions

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: GOBI-FFF was heavily oriented towards maternal and child health: Growth monitoring, ORS for diarrhoea, Breastfeeding, Immunisation, Female education, Food supplementation, and Family planning.

overallFeedback.feedback: Recall the distinction: comprehensive PHC (Alma-Ata) addressed all 8 elements including social determinants, while selective PHC (GOBI-FFF) targeted a few high-impact interventions. Critics said this fragmentation missed the root causes of ill-health.
Right. The comprehensive-vs-selective debate remains relevant: selective PHC achieves quick wins, but without addressing underlying social determinants, the gains may not be sustained.

params.question: A tribal village is located 45 km from the nearest Community Health Centre across unpaved terrain. Families in this village spend over 60% of their health expenditure out-of-pocket. How do these two barriers interact to compound healthcare inaccessibility?

answers.text: They operate independently — resolving either geographic or financial barriers alone would restore adequate healthcare access

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The narration describes these dimensions as 'interacting'. Geographic remoteness increases travel costs and delays, which directly amplify the financial burden — they are not independent problems.

answers.text: Geographic isolation increases travel costs and lost wages, which compound the financial burden of out-of-pocket payments, creating a barrier greater than either alone

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. When families must travel 45 km on unpaved roads, the transport costs, lost wages, and time delay compound the direct out-of-pocket treatment expense. This interaction makes healthcare functionally inaccessible even when a facility technically exists.

answers.text: Financial barriers are the sole determinant — families willing to pay can always access healthcare regardless of distance

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Geographic distance affects access even for those who can afford treatment. Transport delays in obstetric emergencies, snakebites, or acute infections can be fatal regardless of the family's financial capacity.

answers.text: These barriers affect only curative services and do not impair access to preventive or promotive healthcare

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Geographic and financial barriers affect all components of healthcare — preventive services like immunisation, antenatal check-ups, and health education also require physical access to facilities or community health workers.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the three interacting dimensions from the narration: geographic inaccessibility (facility deficits, poor roads), financial inaccessibility (high out-of-pocket expenditure), and their compounding effect — each worsens the other, making healthcare functionally unreachable.
Precisely. India's healthcare access problem is defined by the interaction of its dimensions — geographic, financial, and social — which multiply rather than merely add to each other.
